'''Ronald T. Raines''' is an American chemical biologist. He is the Roger and Georges Firmenich Professor of Natural Products Chemistry at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]]. He is a [[physical organic chemistry|physical organic chemist]] with an interest in [[biology]].

==Education==
Raines was born and raised in the [[New Jersey]] suburbs of [[New York City]]. His father was a Ph.D. chemist, having worked with Charles O. Beckman at [[Columbia University]]. Raines graduated from [[West Essex High School]] in [[North Caldwell, New Jersey]],<ref>[https://cen.acs.org/articles/82/i6/2004-ACS-NATIONAL-AWARD-WINNERS.html "2004 ACS NATIONAL AWARD WINNERS"] Accessed June 15, 2023. “Ronald T. Raines's love of chemistry blossomed during the many long afternoons he spent after school as a teenager, honing his chemistry skills with his teammates on the chemistry team at West Essex (N.J.) High School.”</ref> where he was taught by award-winning chemistry teacher, Rex T. Morrison.<ref>[https://www.njacs.org/education/education-committee "North Jersey Section, American Chemical Society"] Accessed October 27, 2023. "Merrill Award."</ref> He received Sc.B. degrees in chemistry and biology at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], doing undergraduate research with [[Christopher T. Walsh]] on [[pyridoxal phosphate]]-dependent enzymes. He earned A.M. and Ph.D. degrees in chemistry at [[Harvard University]] for work with [[Jeremy R. Knowles]] on catalysis by [[triosephosphate isomerase]]. Also on his Ph.D. thesis committee were [[Walter Gilbert]] and [[Martin Karplus]]. Raines was a [[Helen Hay Whitney Foundation|Helen Hay Whitney]] postdoctoral fellow with [[William J. Rutter]] in the Department of Biochemistry and Biophysics at the [[University of California, San Francisco]], where he cloned and expressed the gene encoding bovine [[pancreatic ribonuclease]].

==Career==
Raines was a member of the faculty at the [[University of Wisconsin–Madison]] from 1989 until 2017. There, he was the [[Henry A. Lardy]] Professor of Biochemistry, [[Linus Pauling]] Professor of Chemical Biology, and a Professor of Chemistry.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chem.wisc.edu/content/national-academy-inventors-and-american-peptide-society-honor-professor-ronald-raines|title=National Academy of Inventors and American Peptide Society Honor Professor Ronald Raines}}</ref> In 2009, he was a Visiting Associate in Chemistry at [[Caltech]]; in 2014, he was the Givaudan–Karrer Distinguished Visiting Professor at the Universität Zürich.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.chem.uzh.ch/en/events/special/GivaudanKarrer.html|title=Givaudan Karrer Lectureships}}</ref> In 2017, he returned to [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]] to join the faculty of his alma mater, [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]]. He is also an Extramural Member of the [[Koch Institute for Integrative Cancer Research]] at MIT, an Affiliate Member of the MIT [[Institute for Medical Engineering and Science]], and an Associate Member of the [[Broad Institute]] of MIT and Harvard. Altogether, he has published more than 450 peer-reviewed journal articles<ref>[https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/?term=raines%20rt National Library of Medicine]</ref> and mentored more than 120 graduate students and postdoctorates.<ref name=chemtree>[https://academictree.org/chemistry/peopleinfo.php?pid=53479 Ronald T. Raines] - Chemistry Tree</ref>

Raines and his coworkers have made the following contributions.
* Exploration of the conformational stability of collagen, which is the most abundant protein in animals.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Collagen structure and stability |journal=Annu. Rev. Biochem. |volume=78 |pages=929–958 |year=2009 |pmid=19344236 |pmc=2846778 |doi=10.1146/annurev.biochem.77.032207.120833 |last1=Shoulders |first1=M. D. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T.}}</ref> The resulting collagen-mimetic peptides are in preclinical trials for the detection and treatment of wounds and fibrosis. This work led to the discovery that ''n''→''π''* interactions<ref>{{cite journal |title=The ''n''→''π''* interaction |journal=Acc. Chem. Res. |volume=50 |pages=1838–1846 |year=2017 |pmid=28735540 |pmc=5559721 |doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.7b00121 |last1=Newberry |first1=R. W. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T.|issue=8 }}</ref> and C5 hydrogen bonds<ref>{{cite journal |title=A prevalent intraresidue hydrogen bond stabilizes proteins |journal=Nat. Chem. Biol. |volume=12 |pages=1084–1088 |year=2016 |pmid=27748749 |pmc=5110370 |doi=10.1038/nchembio.2206 |last1=Newberry |first1=R. W. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T.|issue=12 }}</ref> contribute to the stability of nearly every protein.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Secondary forces in protein folding |journal=ACS Chem. Biol. |volume=14 |pages=1677–1686 |year=2019 |pmid=31243961 |pmc=6995338 |doi=10.1021/acschembio.9b00339 |last1=Newberry |first1=R. W. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T.|issue=8 }}</ref>
* Modifications of human RNA-cleaving enzymes to generate clinical anti-cancer therapies.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Cancer chemotherapy – Ribonucleases to the rescue |journal=Chem. Biol. |volume=8 |pages=405–413 |year=2001 |doi=10.1016/S1074-5521(01)00030-8 |last1=Leland |first1=P. A. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T. |issue=5|pmc=2913432 |pmid=11358688}}</ref> 
* Mechanistic studies on cellular redox homeostasis<ref>{{cite journal |title=Catalysis of protein folding by protein disulfide isomerase and small-molecule mimics |journal=Antioxid. Redox Signal. |volume=5 |pages=413–424 |year=2003 |doi=10.1089/152308603768295159 |pmid=13678529 |last1=Kersteen |first1=E. A. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T. |issue=4|pmc=2814249 }}</ref> and on the uptake of cationic proteins and peptides by mammalian cells.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Internalization of cationic peptides: The road less (or more?) traveled |journal=Cell. Mol. Life Sci. |volume=63 |pages=1819–1822 |year=2006 |pmid=16909213 |pmc=2812862 |doi=10.1007/s00018-006-6170-z |last1=Fuchs |first1=S. M. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T. |issue=16}}</ref>
* New approaches to protein synthesis.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Chemical synthesis of proteins |journal=Annu. Rev. Biophys. Biomol. Struct. |volume=34 |pages=91–118 |year=2005 |pmid=15869385 |pmc=2845543 |doi=10.1146/annurev.biophys.34.040204.144700 |last1=Nilsson |first1=B. L. |last2=Soellner |first2=M. B. |last3=Raines |first3=R. T.}}</ref>
*Novel fluorogenic probes for molecular imaging in living cells.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Bright ideas for chemical biology |journal=ACS Chem. Biol. |volume=3 |pages=142–155 |year=2008 |pmid=18355003 |pmc=2802578 |doi=10.1021/cb700248m |last1=Lavis |first1=L. D. |last2=Raines |first2=R. T. |issue=3}}</ref>
*Methods to convert biomass into useful chemicals.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Biomass to furanics: Renewable routes to chemicals and fuels |journal=ACS Sustain. Chem. Eng. |volume=3 |pages=2591–2605 |year=2015 |doi=10.1021/acssuschemeng.5b00473 |last1=Caes |first1=B. R. |last2=Teixeira |first2=R. E. |last3=Knapp |first3=K. G. |last4=Raines |first4=R. T.|issue=11 }}</ref> 
Raines has served on the editorial advisory boards of various journals and funding panels.
